title: Hantavirus at Sea: MV Hondius Passengers Flown Home from Tenerife
excerpt: A rare Andes virus outbreak aboard a Dutch expedition cruise ship has killed three and triggered a 22-nation repatriation operation from Spain's Canary Islands.
body:
A deadly hantavirus outbreak aboard the Dutch expedition cruise ship MV Hondius reached a critical turning point on May 10, 2026, when the vessel docked at Tenerife's port of Granadilla and a tightly coordinated international evacuation began. All passengers and some crew have now been evacuated from the ship, which was anchored at the Port of Granadilla near the Spanish island of Tenerife.

What Happened Aboard the Hondius: The cruise ship departed from Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1, 2026, and traveled across the South Atlantic Ocean, stopping at several remote locations, including Antarctica, South Georgia Island, Tristan da Cunha, Saint Helena, and Ascension Island. A passenger died from the virus on April 11; his body was removed in Saint Helena, where his wife disembarked before dying two days later in Johannesburg, and a third passenger also died on board. Andes virus, confirmed as the cause of the outbreak, is the only type of hantavirus documented to spread person-to-person, though that spread has typically required close, prolonged contact with a symptomatic person.

The Scale of the Evacuation: A total of 122 individuals were repatriated to their home countries and the Netherlands, including 35 crew members and 87 guests, according to tour operator Oceanwide Expeditions. Seventeen American citizens had been on board during the quarantine period at sea, and a group of 18 people — all of the Americans and one British national residing in the US — were bound for evacuation flights to the United States. One passenger 'tested mildly PCR positive for the Andes virus,' and the passengers were bound for the RESPTC facility at the University of Nebraska Medical Center in Omaha.

Why the WHO Is Urging Calm — and What Comes Next: WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, leading a team in Tenerife, stressed that the risk to the wider public remains low, telling journalists 'this is not another COVID.' WHO currently assesses the risk to the global population from this event as low and will continue to monitor the epidemiological situation. Watch whether any of the exposed passengers — now isolating across more than 20 countries — develop symptoms within the 42-day window, and whether the WHO escalates its risk assessment as new cases are reported.
